The key challenge is not only to identify risky behavior, but to make that knowledge shape the distance a robot uses for long-horizon planning. Existing goal-conditioned methods can compose short behaviors into longer plans, but they usually assume the safety-relevant cost is already known. We introduce CoGeL, a constraint-to-geometry learning method that learns a soft safety signal from robot data and incorporates it directly into the goal-reaching distance used for planning. This makes the learned distance safety-aware, instead of treating safety as a separate classifier, hard mask, or post-hoc filter. We show that errors in the learned safety signal lead to controlled changes in the navigation geometry, that approximate distance consistency supports long-horizon composition through waypoints, and that calibrated safety scores limit the expected number of true violations. Experiments across different navigation tasks show that CoGeL substantially reduces unsafe events while preserving strong long-horizon goal-reaching.
primary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control
secondary_keyword: Robot navigation and locomotion

title: Unified Motion-Action Modeling for Heterogeneous Robot Learning
authors: Yunhao Cao;Shitong Liu;Chao Feng;Meryl Zhang;Xuanchen Lu;Andrew Owens;Kuan Fang
abstract: We present Unified Motion Action (UMA) Model, an approach that uses 3D object motion trajectories as a shared interface to bridge visuomotor control and dynamics modeling. UMA treats object motion and robot actions as co-evolving variables under a masked generative objective, in which the mask pattern determines both the supervision regime during pretraining and the inference mode at deployment. Using hindsight-relabeled motion contexts and a contrastive objective that disentangles task intent from scene geometry, UMA enables multi-task pretraining across heterogeneous data sources without requiring manually annotated task instructions. At deployment, the same pretrained parameters support motion-conditioned visuomotor control, motion-based dynamics modeling, and task adaptation from few-shot demonstrations. Pretrained on publicly available robot demonstrations, human videos, and simulated data, UMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines specialized for each inference mode. Videos and additional details are available at https://uma-robot.github.io
primary_keyword: Robot manipulation
secondary_keyword: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems

title: CS-Pi: Constraint-Satisying Flow Policy Sampling
authors: Soumojit Bhattacharya;Oliver Kroemer;Shubham Tulsiani
abstract: A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint that was absent from its demonstrations, such as a collision-free path or a particular grasp orientation. Existing training-free samplers take one of two approaches. \emph{Guidance} steers the denoising trajectory with a constraint gradient at noisy intermediates: the gradient at a noisy sample need not point toward a clean feasible one. \emph{Projection} maps the finished sample onto the feasible set and executes it: it is efficient, but the result is an action the policy would never draw. We find that this dichotomy need not hold. Our key insight is that the projection is a cheap, clean, feasible signal, and the only mistake is executing it. We introduce Constraint-Satisfying Flow Policy Sampling \texttt{CS-Pi}: we draw from the policy, project the clean sample to the nearest feasible point, and resample from the flow model biased toward that point. Iterating drives the samples toward constraint satisfaction with no noisy-state gradient and no auxiliary network; the method extends to arbitrary costs with a single tweak in the projection function. We evaluate on a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, and a zero-shot Franka deployment. In every setting, \texttt{CS-Pi} stays closest to the policy while satisfying the constraint, and it attains the highest safe-success on a real-world obstacle avoidance task.
primary_keyword: Robot manipulation

title: Unified Whole-Body Control for Quadrupedal Tactile-Informed Loco-Manipulation
authors: Muqun Hu;Yuhao Zhou;Kabir Ray Malik;Chi Lin;Won Suk Lee;Yu She;Yan Gu
abstract: Dynamic loco-manipulation requires legged robots to coordinate whole-body motion while maintaining stable physical interaction with grasped objects under uncertain external forces. While tactile sensing has been widely studied for robotic manipulation, its role in dynamic whole-body control remains largely unexplored. Existing works without tactile feedback commonly grasp firmly rather than regulate the grasp according to the interaction. We propose a tactile-augmented unified reinforcement learning framework that encodes tactile array observations from compliant grippers into a compact latent representation and joins it with proprioception for unified control of the legs, arm, and gripper. With effective grasp stability reward design, the policy learns to simultaneously track body velocity and end-effector trajectories, moderate grasp force, and prevent object slip under both gradual load changes and sudden release events. We deploy the policy zero-shot on a Unitree Go2 with an Interbotix WidowX 250 arm and tactile gripper, demonstrating dynamic tactile-informed loco-manipulation under varying external interactions, achieving a 47% reduction in grasping force and an object drop rate of less than 1%.
primary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control
secondary_keyword: Robot systems, hardware, and sensors for learning

title: PLaW-VLA: Predictive Latent World Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Yu Liu;Hetian Guo;Tianlv Huang;Ziyi Cai;Wudi Chen;Hantang WANG;Qiutong Liu;Yingzhi Peng;Wei Han;Peijun Tang;Jianan Wang;zipei fan;Zhiyuan Zha;Xuan Song
abstract: World models provide predictive priors that are essential for vision-language-action (VLA) policies in long-horizon and dynamic manipulation. However, existing world-model-based VLA methods are often optimized with reconstruction-oriented objectives, which may prioritize low-level visual fidelity over task-relevant state evolution for control. We propose PLaW-VLA, a predictive latent world model for VLA policy learning. Rather than reconstructing future observations in pixel space, PLaW-VLA predicts future world states in a pretrained latent space, providing compact, semantically grounded, and dynamics-aware context for action generation. The model adopts a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture with shared causal self-attention, unifying environment understanding, latent world-state prediction, and action generation within a single sequence-modeling framework. Experiments in simulation and on real robots show that PLaW-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, especially on long-horizon, interaction-rich, and dynamically perturbed tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of latent world-state prediction as a control-aligned objective for generalist robot policy learning.
primary_keyword: Video models and latent world models for robot learning
secondary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

title: Catch Me If You Can: Real-Time Feedback Denoising for Responsive VLAs
authors: Yiheng Ji;Xingru Zhou;Luis Sentis;Mingyo Seo
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by combining semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models with expressive action-generation policies. Diffusion-based action generators are particularly effective for modeling temporally coherent action chunks, but these chunks are typically executed open-loop after inference. This limits responsiveness when objects move, contacts change, or the scene evolves during execution.We propose VLA-Feedback, a two-timescale architecture that combines low-frequency diffusion planning with high-frequency observation feedback. Rather than fully denoising an action chunk before execution, VLA-Feedback stops before the final denoising stage and refines the chunk online using observation-conditioned denoising velocity updates at control frequency. This design preserves the expressiveness of the diffusion planner while enabling real-time action correction without rerunning the full vision-language diffusion model. Experiments on stationary and non-stationary manipulation tasks show that VLA-Feedback preserves static-task performance while improving robustness in dynamic environments.
primary_keyword: Robot manipulation

title: MAPO: Mixture of Experts with Alternating Policy Optimization for Universal Humanoid Motion Tracking
authors: Seonghyeon Lim;Hyeonwoo Lee;Mincheol Kim;Kimin Lee;Hyun Myung
abstract: Universal humanoid motion tracking is essential for enabling humanoid robots to perform diverse tasks in human environments.To capture the wide diversity of human motions, mixture-of-experts (MoE) policies have been widely adopted, leveraging dynamic routing to enhance policy expressiveness. However, we identify that divergence between old and updated policies can be misestimated during policy-gradient updates of MoE policies, due to their dynamic routing. Because most policy-gradient algorithms regulate policy updates based on the divergence, this misestimation can lead to either overly conservative or excessively large updates, which can yield a suboptimal policy. In this paper, we propose Mixture of Experts with Alternating Policy Optimization (MAPO), which alternately optimizes the router and the experts to avoid the divergence misestimation. As a result, MAPO achieves about $1.8\times$ higher reward than an MoE policy trained with an existing policy-gradient method. MAPO also attains the highest tracking success rate among the compared methods and the lowest tracking error across most error metrics, demonstrating its superior performance. Videos can be found on the project website: https://mapo-corl2026.github.io/MAPO/
primary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control

title: Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
authors: Kyeongwon Park;Steven H. Collins
abstract: Subjective user experience is important to human-robot interaction, but the outcomes users value, and how those preferences vary across individuals and contexts, are often unknown. While inverse learning approaches using human data can help identify user rewards, in many assistive settings the experimental costs of executing a control policy, measuring biomechanical or physiological outcomes, and collecting user feedback often limit the number of queries and optimization iterations. Here, we present Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-In-the-Loop Optimization (SFIHILO), which efficiently infers individual-specific reward functions from preferences over human outcomes and identifies a final control policy that maximizes the learned reward. SFIHILO bootstraps a forward model to predict user outcomes from control policies, uses this model for active querying to accelerate inverse reward learning, and then optimizes the final control policy without additional user trials. We score candidate policies by their expected reduction in uncertainty across both forward and inverse beliefs, targeting a regional preference boundary to robustly inform this simultaneous learning process. In simulation, we show that SFIHILO was effective across user heterogeneity, outcome dimensionalities, precision requirements, noise levels, and nonstationarity; compared with mutual information approaches, the proposed active querying strategy significantly improved sample efficiency in inverse learning while preserving forward model accuracy. This approach demonstrates the potential to infer latent human goals, enabling more transferable and effective human-robot interaction.
primary_keyword: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction
secondary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: VoxAfford: Multi-Scale Voxel-Token Fusion for Open-Vocabulary 3D Affordance Detection
authors: Haowen Sun;Shaolong Zhang;Mingyang Li;Chengzhong Ma;Xinzhe Chen;Qiongjie Cui;Xingyu Chen;Zeyang Liu;Xuguang Lan
abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D affordance detection requires localizing interaction regions on point clouds given novel affordance descriptions. Recent methods extend multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with special output tokens that are decoded into segmentation masks. However, these tokens are produced through autoregressive generation, which models sequential dependencies rather than spatial neighborhood relations, leaving them semantically rich but spatially impoverished for 3D localization. We propose Voxel-enhanced Affordance detection (VoxAfford), which bypasses this bottleneck by injecting multi-scale geometric features from a frozen pre-trained 3D VQVAE encoder into the output tokens after generation. Each output token uses its affordance semantics as a query to retrieve relevant geometric patterns from its paired voxel scale via cross-attention, with a learned compatibility gate controlling the injection strength. The enhanced tokens are then aggregated into a spatially-aware affordance prompt through semantic-conditioned attention and propagated alongside per-point features to generate the final mask. Experiments on open-vocabulary affordance detection tasks show that VoxAfford achieves state-of-the-art performance with an approximately 10% absolute improvement in instance-level mIoU, and real robot experiments confirm zero-shot transfer to novel objects.
primary_keyword: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

title: Decision-Centric Counterfactual Preference Optimization for Vision-Language-Action Post-Training
authors: Maocheng Bai;YangJiang;LiaoDaLei;Shengrong Li;WangLin;ShuaihaoWu;Jiashuo Bai
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are increasingly post-trained with rollout-level feedback, but a failed language-conditioned trajectory often hinges on a local decision that the terminal success label does not identify. World models make post-training scalable through imagined rollouts, yet treating the whole trajectory as the supervision unit still mixes object grounding, target selection, contact alignment, and recovery into one outcome. We introduce Decision-Centric Counterfactual Preference Optimization (DCCP), a world-model post-training method that converts imagined futures into localized action preferences. DCCP mines decision-sensitive states using progress curvature and action-token entropy, intervenes only on the current first action chunk under a shared visual-language prefix, and evaluates short counterfactual branches with a conditional progress scorer. High-margin branch differences become action-token preferences optimized by a local DPO-style loss, while a trajectory-level GRPO objective preserves full-task improvement. Across standard LIBERO, LIBERO-BDDL, and MimicGen-D0, DCCP improves average success from 75.6% with WMPO to 80.1%, with the largest gains on instruction-sensitive branch-selection tasks. On four RM65 real-robot tasks, DCCP improves success from 70.6% to 78.8% over WMPO and reduces semantic commitment errors from 13.1% to 7.5%. These results show that world models can provide not only more rollouts, but sharper credit for the action choices that determine downstream progress.
primary_keyword: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
secondary_keyword: Video models and latent world models for robot learning
free_keyword_2: Counterfactual preference learning for robot manipulation

title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
authors: Jonas Eschmann;Giuseppe Loianno
abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator that is focused on high-performance batch rendering and is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. We design a ray-tracing engine that can take full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware (ray-tracing cores) and render RGB and depth observations. HyperDrone supports configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperDrone achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs, while simulating realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.
primary_keyword: Autonomous driving and flight
secondary_keyword: Sim-to-real transfer

title: LiquidLab:  Benchmarking Robotic Automation for Liquid Operation in Laboratory
authors: Yuzhou Wang;Longqi Li;Yang Liu;Yuanhao Wang;Shuyong Gao;Shengyuan Wang;Tianyang Wang;Yue Yao;Min Xu
abstract: Realizing true end-to-end biological laboratory automation requires robotic systems that can support two essential capabilities: directly manipulating liquids, and preparing and clearing the programmable automated liquid-handler platforms through which liquids are ultimately processed. However, existing laboratory benchmarks such as AutoBio and LabUtopia focus on rigid-body instrument operations or chemistry procedures with limited fluid modeling fidelity. We introduce LiquidLab, a robotic benchmark to jointly evaluate physically grounded liquid manipulation and automated liquid-handler operation for biological laboratory automation, comprising sixteen tasks across direct liquid manipulation, platform operations, and long-horizon wet-lab protocols. We further propose a parallel SPH fluid simulation pipeline built on Genesis that enables large-scale parallel liquid simulation on a single GPU, and ground task success in particle-level volumetric criteria rather than pose proxies. Benchmarking four representative imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies reveals that current models remain far from reliable, with failures concentrated in millimeter-scale labware staging and free-surface fluid control, exposing a clear gap between current robotic capabilities and the demands of fully autonomous biology.
primary_keyword: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning

title: Understanding and Mitigating the Video-Action Generalization Gap via Temporal Ratio
authors: Utkarsh Aashu Mishra;Yongxin Chen;Danfei Xu;Yang Liu;Xi Chen;Jiayuan Mao
abstract: Generative video foundation models exhibit strong compositional priors, yet world-action models (WAMs) and video-action models (VAMs) often lose these priors after finetuning on robotic action data. We refer to this discrepancy as the {\bf video-action generalization gap}. In this paper, we systematically investigate this gap by evaluating a comprehensive design space of VAMs, demonstrating that standard design choices yield no emergent explanation pattern. To explain this behavior, we introduce the Temporal Ratio (TR), an attention-based measure of how strongly the action head relies on future latent rollouts relative to the anchored current frame. TR has two key properties: first, a model's structural reliance on future-predictive latents, measured via TR, acts as a predictor of its compositional generalization capacity; second, it natively fluctuates based on task phase, shifting attention to future frames during planning and reverting to the present frame for precise manipulation. Finally, based on these findings, we propose an inference-time adaptive guidance method, which exploits this intrinsic feature attention pattern to dynamically amplify compositional video conditioning signals precisely when the policy relies on future rollouts. Evaluated on the LIBERO benchmark and real-world tasks, our approach mitigates the OOD-ID compositional generalization gap. More details: \url{temporal-ratio.github.io}
primary_keyword: Video models and latent world models for robot learning
secondary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: GUILD: Guided Iterative Data Collection for Imitation Learning
authors: Shivin Dass;Kevin Nguyen;Rohan Yelandur;Junhong Xu;Roberto Martín-Martín
abstract: Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision–language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists.
primary_keyword: Robotic data generation
secondary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: Inference-time Policy Steering via Vision and Touch
authors: Yilin Wu;Zilin Si;Zeynep Temel;Oliver Kroemer;Andrea Bajcsy
abstract: Inference-time steering adapts pre-trained generative robot policies during deployment by verifying candidate actions before execution. While prior methods typically perform this verification only with visual observations, vision alone is often insufficient for contact-rich manipulation, where success depends on both global task progress and subtle local interactions such as contact force. We introduce ViTaL, a visuo-tactile inference-time steering framework that formulates multimodal guidance as a bi-level optimization problem. At the high level, visual sampling-and-verification performs long-horizon mode selection, deciding what behavior the robot should execute. At the low level, tactile-guided diffusion editing refines the selected action sequence over a shorter horizon to satisfy local contact requirements. To support outcome-based steering, ViTaL learns a visuo-tactile latent world model and employs semantically aligned visual and tactile verifiers, including a novel text-conditioned tactile reward that scores predicted tactile futures directly in latent space. Across three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, ViTaL improves overall success by 51% over the base policy, outperforms unimodal steering by at least 33%, and exceeds naive multimodal fusion by at least 20%. Website: corl2026vital.github.io.
primary_keyword: Robot manipulation
secondary_keyword: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

title: Diagnosing Compositional Generalization in Sequential Robot Tasks
authors: Yixiao Wang;Cheng-En Wu;Lingfeng Sun;Pengcheng Wang;Xiang Ji;Boyuan Liang;Guojian Zhan;Masayoshi Tomizuka
abstract: Sequential robot manipulation requires policies to execute novel combinations of familiar instruction components. However, collecting demonstrations for all possible instruction tuples is combinatorially expensive, while sparsely covered datasets often fail under out-of-distribution recombination. This paper studies compositional generalization through the lens of instruction-space coverage. We decompose the generalization gap into three sources: marginal instruction shift, instruction-compositional shift, and context--action shift. This decomposition allows us to diagnose when sparse training coverage is sufficient, and what structure the training set must preserve for reliable action prediction. Our results show that exhaustive tuple enumeration is unnecessary: a structured subset, as small as one quarter of the full task space, can recover strong out-of-distribution performance when it covers action-relevant dependencies. We further find that sparse training often fails due to instruction steering rather than missing low-level skills; finetuning only one demonstration per task improves OOD success from 0.4% to 54.7%. For semantically dependent tasks, effective coverage must capture relational structure rather than only factor diversity. These findings suggest that efficient robot data collection should prioritize dependency coverage in instruction space over exhaustive task expansion. More results are available in the supplementary material. Code and datasets will be released soon.
primary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: ObstaDiff: Generalizable Diffusion Policy Learning via Obstacle-aware Representations
authors: Jiawen Wang;Kevin Yao;M. Khalid Jawed
abstract: Imitation learning has achieved impressive results in robotic manipulation, yet most existing approaches assume clean backgrounds and lack explicit mechanisms for obstacle-aware motion generation. Extending such policies to cluttered, real-world scenes with unstructured obstacles remains a key generalization challenge. We present ObstaDiff, a decomposed diffusion-policy framework with a lightweight obstacle-aware visual encoder. ObstaDiff extracts a structured target--obstacle--background representation, enabling the downstream alignment policy to generate end-effector trajectories toward a target-centered bottleneck pose while reasoning about surrounding obstacles. We evaluate ObstaDiff on 61 real-robot greenhouse trials spanning target-pose, obstacle-layout, and target-appearance generalization. ObstaDiff achieves 75.41% average task success and 8.20% average obstacle collision rate, outperforming representative imitation-learning baselines and improving generalization in cluttered agricultural scenes.
primary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)
secondary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

title: StressDream: Steering Video World Models for Robust Policy Evaluation and Improvement
authors: Junwon Seo;Sushant Veer;Ran Tian;Wenhao Ding;Apoorva Sharma;Karen Leung;Edward Schmerling;Marco Pavone;Andrea Bajcsy
abstract: Video world models (WMs) have shown promise for policy evaluation and improvement by imagining realistic future observations conditioned on ego-robot actions. While WMs can model distributions over futures, policy evaluation and improvement typically rely on nominal imaginations, which can miss high-impact outcomes of robot actions unless prohibitively many samples are drawn. To enable robust policy evaluation and improvement over WM imaginations, we propose StressDream, which steers imaginations toward high-impact yet plausible outcomes specified at inference time by optimizing the initial noise of diffusion-based WMs. However, optimizing high-dimensional noise is challenging: the optimization must reason about nuanced, scene-dependent target events in generated videos while avoiding out-of-distribution (OOD) noise that yields implausible imaginations. We address this with two complementary objectives: a semantic objective with a Vision-Language Model that provides informative gradients by reasoning about the generated video, and a plausibility objective that prevents the optimized noise from drifting OOD. With state-of-the-art video world models for autonomous driving and robotic manipulation, we show that StressDream effectively steers imaginations toward high-impact yet plausible outcomes specified by text at inference time, such as task failures, enabling robust policy evaluation and improvement by identifying actions whose plausible futures include undesirable outcomes. Video results can be found at https://stressdream.github.io/.
primary_keyword: Video models and latent world models for robot learning
secondary_keyword: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming

title: CoSMO: Conformal Semantic Mapping for Open-World Safe Robot Navigation
authors: Shuqi Wang;Yiwei Zheng;Pingrui Zhang;Yue Gao;Xiang Yin
abstract: Safe autonomous navigation requires not only geometric obstacle avoidance but also semantic awareness. Different object categories demand different safety clearances, and the set of relevant categories may expand as the robot explores novel environments.  Vision-language models (VLMs) offer rich semantic representations for building maps of unknown scenes, yet their confidence scores are poorly calibrated, making raw predictions unreliable for safety-critical planning. Conformal prediction (CP) can provide coverage guarantees, but existing methods assume a fixed label set and stationary data, limiting their use in open-world settings. We propose Conformal Semantic Mapping for Open-World Safe Robot Navigation (CoSMO), a semantic safety mapping framework that transforms VLM embeddings into calibrated coverage sets and safety-aware obstacle dilations over a dynamically expanding hazard vocabulary, even under distribution shift. Experiments on the Matterport3D (MP3D) dataset show that CoSMO reduces semantic collisions by 61.6% relative to a geometry-only baseline, while maintaining formal coverage guarantees even under delayed expert feedback. Code will be released upon publication.
primary_keyword: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems
secondary_keyword: Robot navigation and locomotion

title: ELASTIC: Efficiently Learning to Adaptively Scale Test-Time Compute for Generative Control Policies
authors: Andrew Zou Li;Gokul Swamy;Yonatan Bisk;Andrea Bajcsy
abstract: Generative control policies (GCPs), such as diffusion policies and flow-based vision-language-action models, enable test-time scaling in robot control. This compute can be allocated along two axes: *sequential scaling*, which increases denoising steps to refine actions, and *parallel scaling*, which samples multiple candidate actions to search across modes of the policy distribution. Existing methods typically rely on fixed conservative schedules that may over-compute in easy states and under-allocate in difficult ones. However, the optimal allocation is hard to know a priori as it is state-, task-, and policy-dependent: early stages of a grasp may benefit from broader parallel exploration, while near-contact phases may require more sequential refinement for precision. We present ELASTIC, an algorithm that learns state-dependent test-time compute schedules for GCPs. We formulate compute allocation as a meta-Markov Decision Process in which a meta-policy interacts with a frozen pretrained robot policy and selects sequential steps and parallel samples at each denoising iteration to maximize task success while minimizing compute. Using reinforcement learning, this meta-policy also learns adaptive compute schedules without access to the GCP's training data. Across simulated manipulation benchmarks with diffusion policies, ELASTIC Pareto-dominates fixed and single-axis scaling baselines at matched compute budgets. On real-world robot manipulation with the $\pi_{0.5}$ vision-language-action model, ELASTIC matches best-of-$10$ success while reducing wall-clock latency by 34%.
primary_keyword: Combination of learning and planning in robotics
secondary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control

title: On the Limits of Sampling-Based Reachability: Geometry, Dynamics, and Sample Complexity
authors: Jixian Liu;Ihab Tabbara;Hussein Sibai;Enrique Mallada
abstract: Reachability analysis is central to safety-critical control, robotics, and neural network verification, but classical computational methods, such as Hamilton--Jacobi reachability and set propagation, scale poorly with state dimension. Sampling-based methods have emerged as a promising alternative, often providing finite-sample guarantees that bound the probability-mass left uncovered. However, an explicit account of how the geometry of the initial set, the dynamics, and the sampling law affect the accuracy of the estimator is not fully available in the literature. We study this by casting sampling-based reachable-set recovery as geometric support estimation over a family of problems specified by an initial set, its dynamics, and a sampling law. First, we identify two regularity properties, positive reach of the initial set's complement and Lipschitz continuity of the dynamics, that together make recovery well-posed: a probability-mass coverage guarantee can be upgraded to accuracy $r$ in Hausdorff distance. Second, we bound the resulting sample complexity: recovery is achievable with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\big((e^{3LT}/r)^n\big)$ samples, exponential in both the state dimension and the time horizon. Third, we show that neither can be removed: an almost-matching minimax lower bound of $\Omega\!\big((e^{LT}/r)^n\big)$ holds for every estimator, so the exponential dependence on dimension and the degradation over the horizon are both intrinsic, not artifacts of a particular method. Experiments on nonlinear systems confirm that adversarial sampling improves constants but not the scaling.
primary_keyword: Theoretical foundations of robot learning
secondary_keyword: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems

title: Hardware-as-Regularization: Enhancing Data Consistency in Imitation Learning via an Adjustable Passive Compliant Leader Arm
authors: Hideyuki Ichiwara;Yushi Kaida;Hirokazu Ishida
abstract: While low-cost passive leader arms enable scalable data collection for imitation learning, their lack of restoring forces causes unconstrained redundant degrees of freedom, resulting in highly inconsistent joint-space trajectories. To address this without relying on expensive active actuators, we propose a novel, low-cost passive joint mechanism featuring an adjustable mechanical clutch and a 3D-printed spiral spring. This mechanism introduces ``Hardware-as-Regularization'' by providing adjustable mechanical compliance that acts as a physical prior. By naturally guiding redundant joints back to a user-defined zero-point, our system significantly improves kinematic consistency without increasing the operator's cognitive load. Experimental results demonstrate that our purely mechanical approach drastically reduces joint-angle variance compared to a naive passive arm, achieving trajectory consistency on par with a more complex, active virtual spring system. Furthermore, in downstream policy learning, our mechanism stabilizes demonstrations by eliminating manual drift compensation, thereby matching the task success rates of the active setup while preserving extreme cost-effectiveness.
primary_keyword: Robot systems, hardware, and sensors for learning
secondary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: SCAPE: Scenario-Conditioned Simulation-Augmented Policy Evaluation
authors: Dijie Zhu;Seunghun Oh;Ruopeng Huang;Zhiyu Huang;Jiaqi Ma;Chen Tang
abstract: Reliable performance evaluation is a central bottleneck for deploying robot-learning policies in real-world conditions. Real-world testing produces faithful evaluation but is costly and difficult to scale, whereas simulation-based testing is easy to scale but inevitably biased due to the sim-to-real gap. Neither source alone is sufficient for scalable and reliable policy evaluation. This motivates simulation-augmented policy evaluation, which combines limited real-world rollouts with abundant simulation proxies for sample-efficient performance estimation. Yet, existing methods focus on estimating performance averaged over initial conditions and deployment settings. By construction, such population-level averages collapse scenario-specific variation, providing limited information about when and where a policy can be safely deployed. To address this limitation, we propose SCAPE, a scenario-conditioned simulation-augmented policy evaluation framework that instead predicts scenario-conditioned real-world policy performance from limited paired sim-and-real evaluation samples and large-scale simulation-based testing rollouts. SCAPE corrects the sim-to-real bias in the simulation labels before using them to train the prediction model, and calibrates the prediction uncertainty through conformal prediction. We validate SCAPE on two embodied task domains, autonomous driving and quadruped velocity tracking. In sim-to-sim settings, it reduces the scenario-level performance prediction error by 4.9%/34.7% in driving and 14.5%/27.7% in quadruped velocity tracking relative to scene-conditioned neural baselines and aggregate statistical baselines on average. We also validate SCAPE for evaluating a velocity-tracking policy deployed on a physical Unitree Go2. In addition, SCAPE improves testing sample-efficiency, produces narrower calibrated prediction intervals, enhances generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios, and unlocks fine-grained deployment strategies.
primary_keyword: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming
secondary_keyword: Autonomous driving and flight

title: C³ache: Accelerating World Action Models with Cross Inference Chunk Cache
authors: Weisen Zhao;Lam Christopher Nguyen;Zhicong Lu;Yuzhang Shang
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) generalize better than standard Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to novel motions and environments, because a video-modeling objective lets them learn from abundant unlabeled video rather than scarce labeled robot demonstrations. This generalization is computationally expensive. To complete a task, a WAM runs over multiple inference chunks, and each chunk requires a costly denoising process. Existing acceleration methods reduce this cost by caching and reusing computation within a single chunk's denoising trajectory. Our empirical analysis reveals a substantial source of redundancy they overlook: redundancy across chunks. When a robot executes a smooth behavior, the residuals computed at a given denoising step are strongly correlated from one chunk to the next. We introduce C³ache, a training-free method that caches and reuses these residuals across inference chunks at the same denoising step. Experiments on benchmarks with a Fast-WAM backbone show that C³ache achieves up to a 2.5X speedup in total wall-clock inference time, with negligible degradation in task success rate.
primary_keyword: Video models and latent world models for robot learning

title: Robustness without Wrinkles: Parallel Simulation and Robust MPC for Certified Deformable Manipulation
authors: Wei-Chen Li;Jeffrey Fang;Sasanka Polisetti;Yuexi Song;Glen Chou
abstract: We present CORD-SLS, a real-time control method for safe deformable object manipulation, with a focus on ropes and cloth. At its core is a GPU-parallel differentiable simulator with contact smoothing which enables efficient gradient-based planning through intermittent contact. To robustly satisfy constraints under model and sensing uncertainty, we develop a real-time, GPU-parallel output-feedback robust model predictive control (MPC) algorithm that plans with this simulator. We further show that the simulator accelerates model-based RL for training neural manipulation policies. To improve real-world robustness, we use conformal prediction to calibrate visual-feedback and perception-error bounds for MPC, producing reachable tubes that enable high-probability safe control. We evaluate CORD-SLS on high-dimensional, contact-rich rope and cloth manipulation tasks in simulation and hardware, including obstacle avoidance, routing, folding, and smoothing. Across settings, CORD-SLS achieves millisecond-speed planning, exceeding baselines in safety, speed, and task success.
primary_keyword: Robot manipulation
secondary_keyword: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems

title: AnyRank: Reliable Anytime Policy Ranking via Sequential Testing
authors: Apurva Badithela;David Snyder;Tenny Yin;Jade Sceats;George J. Pappas;Nikolai Matni;Masha Itkina;Haruki Nishimura;Anirudha Majumdar
abstract: Due to the high cost of hardware experiments, robot policies are predominantly evaluated by comparing their empirical performance on a limited number of hardware trials. However, finite-sample statistical uncertainty can lead to erroneous conclusions, especially when ranking multiple policies using a fixed batch of evaluation data. We propose \algname: a \emph{sequential} method for policy ranking that (i) \emph{adaptively allocates trials} to hard-to-separate policies, (ii) provides (partial) rankings at \emph{any stopping time} while bounding the probability of an incorrect ranking, and (iii) optionally \emph{exploits prior information} to prioritize hardware evaluations more efficiently using a small set of held-out hardware evaluations or rollouts in a world model. We achieve these properties through novel theoretical contributions that combine sequential and multiple-hypothesis testing. Experiments in simulation and real-world policy evaluation benchmarks show that \algname requires up to 50% fewer hardware evaluations compared to existing statistically rigorous approaches, while guarding against the incorrect rankings produced by heuristic methods used by state-of-the-art benchmarks.
primary_keyword: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming

title: Scalable Behavior Cloning with Open Data, Training, and Evaluation
authors: Arthur Allshire;Himanshu Gaurav Singh;Ritvik Singh;Adam Rashid;Hongsuk Choi;David McAllister;Justin Yu;Yiyuan Chen;Huang Huang;Pieter Abbeel;Xi Chen;Rocky Duan;Phillip Isola;Jitendra Malik;Fred Shentu;Guanya Shi;Philipp Wu;Angjoo Kanazawa
abstract: We introduce ABC, a fully open-source stack for manipulation with behavior cloning. At its core is ABC-Data: the largest open-source, bimanual teleoperation dataset to date, featuring 3,500 hours of data spanning over 130K episodes across 195 diverse tasks. Furthermore, we open-source our accessible hardware setup, training infrastructure, and simulation pipeline. We also release 280 hours of sim-teleop data and provide a co-training recipe that produces correlated simulation and real-world evaluation. This allows researchers to effectively evaluate design choices without deploying on physical robots. We explore various training recipes and compare common architectural choices for Diffusion Transformers (DiT) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, grounding our findings in real-world evaluations. The resulting policies successfully execute dexterous tasks such as box folding and extracting credit cards from wallets. By providing a reproducible toolkit, we aim to place researchers on an equal footing, establishing the necessary foundation to learn the ABCs of Behavior Cloning together as a community.
primary_keyword: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
secondary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: Automating the Design of Embodied Agent Architectures
authors: Jian Zhou;Sihao Lin;Jin Li;Shuai Fu;Gengze Zhou;Qi Wu
abstract: Embodied agents are typically built as hand-designed compositions of perception, memory, planning, and action modules. This modularity exposes a large architectural design space, but current systems still rely on researcher intuition to choose where information is stored, how observations are processed, and how model calls are connected. Agent Architecture Search (AAS) automates such design for text-domain agents, but has not been systematically evaluated on perceptual embodied agents through simulator rollouts. We study this transfer. We introduce AgentCanvas, a typed-graph runtime that hosts embodied executors as editable node-and-wire programs with simulator-aware execution and episode-level logs, and KDLoop, a coding-agent search procedure that cycles through proposal, critique, experiment, and distillation, with triggered reflection after stalls. We evaluate three AAS variants across four embodied executors spanning navigation, embodied question answering, and language-conditioned manipulation. The resulting 3×4 matrix shows that architecture-level search can produce deployable and directional success-rate gains on embodied tasks, while one apparent high-scoring candidate is rejected as leak-bearing. At the same time, the experiments expose constraints that are muted in text-domain AAS: optimization signals can be masked by rollout noise, search can become trapped in local edit basins, and episode-level credit assignment only partially emerges even when detailed logs are available. These results characterize both the promise and the current limits of automated architecture search for embodied agents.
primary_keyword: Combination of learning and planning in robotics
secondary_keyword: Task and motion planning

title: Trajectory-Level Redirection Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Gokul Puthumanaillam;Vardhan Dongre;Pranay Thangeda;Hooshang Nayyeri;Dilek Hakkani-Tür;Melkior Ornik
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bring natural language into closed-loop robot control, enabling robots to execute manipulation tasks directly from text instructions. The same interface gives text a recurring role in control because the prompt is reused at every replanning step, and each prompt-conditioned action changes the future observations on which the policy acts. Existing VLA attacks study adversarial prompts that elicit targeted low-level actions or make such actions persist across changing images. We identify a stronger trajectory-level failure mode: a prompt that still $\textit{appears}$ to specify the intended task but redirect the final physical outcome. We mathematically formalize this setting as $\textit{command-preserving trajectory redirection}$, a prompt-only threat model in which the attacker chooses one prompt before the episode, all policy and environment components remain fixed, and the prompt must stay close to the benign instruction while omitting target words and correction language. To find such prompts, we introduce an on-policy prompt search method that uses rollouts to discover perturbations whose closed-loop behavior tracks a target task while satisfying the command-preserving constraints. Experiments in simulation and on hardware show that near-benign prompt perturbations can redirect VLA rollouts to attacker-specified targets. These results expose a trajectory-level vulnerability in VLA instruction grounding: text that appears to preserve the intended command can still give an adversary control over the robot's final physical outcome.
primary_keyword: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems
secondary_keyword: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems

title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
authors: Liqian Ma;Vaibhav Saxena;Utkarsh Aashu Mishra;Shuo Cheng;Yongxin Chen;Danfei Xu
abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate Active Generative Simulation: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility simulation parameter distributions without human heuristics. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable.
primary_keyword: Robotic data generation
secondary_keyword: Sim-to-real transfer

title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
authors: Pranav Teegavarapu;Sriyash Poddar;Rico Qi;Cleah Winston;Krisha Khandelwal;Natasha Jaques;Abhishek Gupta
abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through an analysis of intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Driven by these insights, we identify shortcomings in prior methods for learning from interventions and propose Q-OIL, a method that introduces optimistic bonuses on intervention transitions in reinforcement learning, encouraging the agent to revisit and learn from informative intervention states. We show that with the right design choices, including decoupled critics to avoid over-optimism and imitation-learning regularization, our proposed method learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real-world robotic tasks. By grounding both evaluation and learning in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.
primary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control
secondary_keyword: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction

title: BarrierFormer: Transformer-Guided Predictive Barrier Enforcement for Safe Robot Control
authors: Anandsingh Chauhan;Kunal Garg
abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have become one of the most popular tools for encoding and enforcing state constraints in safety-critical robotics. Standard CBF approaches are inherently myopic in nature as they enforce safety only at the current time step. Consequently, the system can be driven toward the boundary of the safe set where no feasible safe control exists at a future timestep. Model predictive control (MPC) based approaches address this by enforcing state constraints over a receding horizon. However, such approaches require solving a constrained optimization problem at every step, which is computationally expensive for real-time deployment. We propose BarrierFormer, a barrier-supervised transformer framework that addresses these limitations by encoding rollout-level CBF constraints in learning a safe policy. A causal transformer encodes observation-action history, outputs a residual correction to a nominal controller through the action head, and autoregressively generates a predictive rollout through the dynamics head. A barrier critic operating on local observations evaluates CBF constraint violations along this rollout, and a safety teacher computes barrier-consistent actions satisfying these constraints as direct supervision targets for the control policy. During inference, the policy maps observation-action history to control actions without any online optimization, enabling real-time usage of the proposed history-based predictive safety enforcement. Evaluations across linear and nonlinear dynamical systems for safe goal-directed navigation show that BarrierFormer outperforms reinforcement learning (RL)-based, diffusion-based, MPC-based, and transformer-based baselines in safety rate, success rate, and inference latency.
primary_keyword: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems
secondary_keyword: Model-based and model-free learning for robotic control

title: UniFlow: A Unified Multi-Modal Policy for Robot Manipulation
authors: Ge Yan;Shun Iwase;Yuzhi Fan;Dieter Fox;Sergey Zakharov;Katherine Liu
abstract: Visuomotor manipulation policies face a persistent trade-off: image-only policies inherit the semantic priors of large-scale 2D pretraining but are brittle to lighting, texture, and viewpoint shift, whereas 3D-only policies are robust to such factors yet are often trained from scratch. Some recent multi-modal policies combine both streams but typically process 3D through a from-scratch encoder, preserving this asymmetry. We present UniFlow, a unified 2D+3D co-training recipe for manipulation in which 3D observations are represented as image-shaped pointmaps so that pretrained 2D backbones can be used to encode both modalities, and RGB and pointmap streams are fused by a unified diffusion transformer with per-modality modulation. On average across thirteen dexterous manipulation tasks from the challenging LBM simulation benchmark, UniFlow outperforms a strong RGB-only baseline in a distribution-shifted setting. UniFlow also outperforms the generalist VLA $\pi_{0.5}$ when averaged over five RoboTwin bimanual tasks as well as four real-world YAM tasks.
primary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)
secondary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

title: Exploring the Intrinsic Geometry of Diffusion Models with Constrained Inverse Kinematics
authors: Phone Thiha Kyaw;Miguel Rogel-García;Jonathan Kelly
abstract: Recent studies suggest that diffusion models can recover geometric structure in the data manifolds they are trained on, yet the supporting evidence has so far come mostly from natural-image data, where the underlying geometry itself is unknown. We study this question in a setting where the geometry is analytically tractable: constrained inverse kinematics (IK). Each task-space constraint defines a configuration-space manifold with known intrinsic dimension, giving direct ground truth for evaluating the geometry learned by the model. For each of the 6-DoF UR5 and 7-DoF Franka, we train a single conditional diffusion model across seven constraint families, spanning solution manifolds from discrete IK branches to self-motion manifolds. Our empirical results reveal that the intrinsic dimension recovered from the model's score function matches the analytical degrees of freedom of the corresponding constraint manifold across both robots. Moreover, linear interpolation in the latent space leads to generated solutions that remain close to the appropriate constraint manifold, indicating that the learned representation further captures geometric structure of the constraint family beyond intrinsic dimension alone. Constrained IK therefore offers a controlled setting for studying the intrinsic geometry learned by diffusion models.
primary_keyword: Theoretical foundations of robot learning
secondary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

title: Drifting on Demand: A Profiled-Likelihood Transformer for Online Parameter Estimation
authors: Alex Matsumura;Jonathan Y.M. Goh
abstract: In real-world environments, fast and accurate adaptation of dynamics models is a fundamental challenge for model-based online control. This is exemplified in autonomous drifting, where effective vehicle parameters shift rapidly with tire temperature, surface friction, tire wear, and load transfer. Prediction errors from the dynamics model in this regime differ in scale across state channels and vary across driving regimes, making fixed squared-error objectives brittle. Likelihood objectives naturally account for this structure, but joint negative log-likelihood training of dynamics parameters and residual variances is often unstable. We address this limitation using a decoupled profiled-likelihood objective for training history-conditioned structured dynamics estimators directly from observed state-control transitions. Using this objective, we train a bidirectional transformer that aggregates long state-control histories through a learned query token and outputs parameters of a structured vehicle dynamics model in a single forward pass. The resulting estimator runs at over 100Hz and is integrated into an existing MPC framework. We evaluate the approach on two full-scale vehicles, a heavily modified Toyota Supra and a Lexus LC500, across multiple drifting experiments with varying operating conditions. Our estimator improves tracking over hand-tuned physics and neural-network dynamics baselines, achieving up to 2.4 times lower RMS path-tracking error. These results show that profiled likelihood-based parameter adaptation can reliably and efficiently improve closed-loop performance in real-world applications of model-based control.
primary_keyword: Autonomous driving and flight
secondary_keyword: Model-based and model-free learning for robotic control

title: MDF++: Visuo-Tactile World Action Model with End-to-end Representation Learning
authors: Zixuan Huang;Jinhao Yu;Zachary S. Charlick;Dmitry Berenson
abstract: Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physically-grounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. We evaluate MDF++ on a suite of contact-rich manipulation tasks, including real-world bolt screwing and nut mating, and show that it outperforms WAMs built on frozen pretrained representations by up to 50%.
primary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
secondary_keyword: Video models and latent world models for robot learning

title: Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos
authors: Bhawna Paliwal;Haritheja Etukuru;William Liang;Pieter Abbeel;Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah;Jitendra Malik
abstract: How can we scalably generate data for robotic manipulation, especially on human-like platforms such as dexterous multi-fingered hands? Learning from watching human videos has recently emerged as a likely answer to this question. However, difficulties in estimating hand-object interaction and crossing the human-to-robot embodiment gap have hindered the adoption of abundant monocular RGB-only human videos as the primary source of robot manipulation data. In this work, we present Do as I Do, an algorithm to reconstruct and retarget monocular RGB human videos to multi-fingered dexterous robotic hands. Do as I Do reconstructs hand-object interactions from various egocentric and exocentric in-the-wild video sources. Do as I Do then retargets these hand-object interaction estimates into a sequence of actions executable in the real world, yielding robot-complete manipulation data from disparate human videos. Overall, Do as I Do outperforms previous state of the art in estimating hand-object interactions and extracting dexterous manipulation trajectories from RGB videos, as we show on experiments on datasets with ground truths and on a dataset of video clips collected online. Finally, our experiments enable us to propose an efficacy playbook for practitioners collecting human data for manipulation.
primary_keyword: Robotic data generation
secondary_keyword: Robot manipulation

title: CrowdMAPS: Crowdsourcing Multiple Actions per State for Real-World Robot Imitation Learning
authors: Yilong Song;Harshvardhan Chandirasekar;Karthik Desingh;Chen Zhu-Tian
abstract: Real-world robot imitation learning is often limited by the cost of collecting physical demonstrations, which typically yield only one action label per visited state. We present CrowdMAPS, a web-based crowdsourcing paradigm for augmenting real-robot datasets with Multiple Actions per State (MAPS). After or during standard robot data collection, CrowdMAPS distributes visited robot states to remote annotators through a web-based 3D interface, where they specify alternative valid actions without requiring access to physical robot hardware. This expands robot datasets along a complementary “width” dimension — by increasing the number of actions per visited state — rather than only by collecting more trajectories. We evaluate CrowdMAPS using keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations supplied by non-expert annotators and train imitation policies on the resulting MAPS data. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing MAPS width from one to ten actions per state improves sample efficiency and increases average success rates by 35.6% for keypose policies and 33.0% for trajectory policies. These results show that software-mediated human annotations can augment physical robot data to afford denser supervision, establishing CrowdMAPS as a scalable digital layer for real-robot data collection.
primary_keyword: Robotic data generation
secondary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: TacStyle: Personalizing Tactile Robot Policies using Structured Behavior Representations
authors: Kevin Robledo;Matías I. Torres Galaz;Kumar Dixhant Rai;Shelly Sara Ulman;Tasmia Tasrin;Heramb Nemlekar
abstract: Robotic systems that assist humans should be capable of adapting their behaviors to individual user preferences. For instance, users may want a robot arm to adjust the amount of force it applies while folding their laundry or cleaning furniture. Natural language provides an intuitive way for humans to communicate such preferences. Recent progress in language-conditioned robot policies has shown that robots can successfully use language prompts to determine what task to perform. However, extending the same approach to realize how the task should be performed requires detailed labels describing the preferences or styles of trajectories in the task data. Not only is collecting such annotations challenging, but conditioning directly on these labels may also fail to provide fine-grained control over a continuous range of behaviors. For example, it can be difficult to convey the exact force that a robot must apply through abstract instructions like "apply a bit more pressure than before". Therefore, in this work, we propose using language to reason over preferred behaviors instead of directly generating them. We first learn a structured latent representation that organizes user preferences according to differences in the corresponding trajectories. Then, given a preference prompt, we use a foundation model to interpret this latent space and choose a value that produces the desired behavior. Through both simulation and real-world experiments, we show that selecting robot behaviors from an intuitively structured latent space enables more precise adaptation to user preferences while requiring significantly fewer preference labels than language-conditioned policies.
primary_keyword: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction
secondary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)

title: DIQL:Distributional Implicit Q Learning for Offline to Online Reinforcement Learning
authors: Weiran Liao;C F Maximilian Nagy;Ge Li;Onur Celik;Hongyi Zhou;Andreas Loehr;Qian Wang;Longrui Chen;Yucheng Tang;Tao Chen;Gerhard Neumann
abstract: A central challenge in offline reinforcement learning is ensuring that value updates remain grounded in the support of the dataset. Querying a learned critic at out-of-distribution actions can lead to overestimated values, which, unlike in the online setting, cannot be corrected through further interaction. A prominent strategy is to fit the value function using only in-distribution data while approximating an upper expectile of action values to induce optimism. We retain this in-distribution principle but reconsider how optimism is obtained. Instead of estimating an expectile through an asymmetric regression loss, we use a categorical critic representation, where an optimistic target can be obtained simply by selecting an upper quantile of the learned value distribution. Crucially, this distributional perspective allows optimism to be calibrated according to evidence, with the quantile level adapted on a per-state basis. States with well-supported value distributions are treated more optimistically, whereas states with weaker evidence are assigned more conservative value estimates. We call our method Distributional Implicit Q-Learning for offline-to-online reinforcement learning (DIQL). Across four representative robot task suites from OGBench, DIQL outperforms state-of-the-art offline RL methods. On Robomimic tasks, we further show that DIQL naturally extends to robot offline-to-online fine-tuning.
primary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control

title: Learning Robust Visuomotor Policies via Dynamics Alignment
authors: Dohyeok Lee;Jung Min Lee;Munkyung Kim;Seokhun Ju;Jin Woo Koo;Kyungjae Lee;Dohyeong Kim;Taehyun Cho;Tapomayukh Bhattacharjee;Jungwoo Lee
abstract: Generative BC policies model expert action distributions well, but they do not explicitly reason about what scene a candidate action would produce, so they cannot tell whether it reaches a task-relevant state. We address this by coupling action generation with an action-conditioned dynamics model that predicts the future observations induced by actions. However, naively placing such a dynamics model inside a generative policy creates a circular dependency. Future observations are needed to guide action generation, yet those observations can only be predicted from the action samples being generated. We introduce Dynamics-Aligned Flow Matching Policy (DAP), where a flow matching policy and an action-conditioned flow matching dynamics model co-sample actions and future observations through flow extrapolation. At each step the two flows correct each other, and the samples converge to a self-consistent action and future pair on which the policy and dynamics model agree. Across four simulated tasks and three real-world tasks, DAP achieves the highest average success rate, with relative improvements of 47.0% in simulation and 34.0% in the real world over the strongest baseline in each setting. Moreover, when the future-observation estimate is corrupted at inference time, DAP recovers a self-consistent action-future pair through iterative refinement, whereas video-conditioned and post-hoc dynamics baselines, which use a fixed future surrogate, degrade or fail.
primary_keyword: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)
secondary_keyword: Robot manipulation

title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
authors: Qiayuan Liao;Yiyang Shao;Junfeng Long;Kevin Zakka;Roberto Horowitz;Pieter Abbeel;Koushil Sreenath
abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute.SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient.In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline.  After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures.From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions.SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.
primary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control
secondary_keyword: Model-based and model-free learning for robotic control

title: Unsupervised Actuator Networks as a Residual World Model for Humanoid Control
authors: Nolan Fey;Khai Nguyen;Yash Prabhu;Gabriel B. Margolis;Pulkit Agrawal
abstract: Humanoid behavior learning uses either physical simulations, which generalize to diverse motions but have limited fidelity, or neural world models, which are highly expressive but data-hungry and brittle. Residual world modeling retains the strengths of both: it preserves the first-principles priors of the physics simulator and only learns the sim-to-real gap. A key challenge when training the residual model for humanoids is accurately initializing the floating base state and contact forces in the simulator to match recorded hardware states. Using the Unsupervised Actuator Networks (UAN) formulation, our method learns a residual correction without torque sensing or motion capture by using a novel proprioceptive state estimator to align initial contact forces and base velocities during open-loop playback of hardware trajectories. This alignment allows the model to capture physics discrepancies rather than artifacts from inconsistent simulator initialization. The resulting residual simulator constrains downstream policy learning to actuator-feasible motions, improving sim-to-real transfer robustness, and enabling efficient locomotion and precise end-effector force control on hardware.
primary_keyword: Sim-to-real transfer
secondary_keyword: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control

title: Robot-DIFT: Correspondence-Sensitive Diffusion Features for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
authors: Yu Deng;Yufeng Jin;Xiaogang Jia;Jiahong Xue;Gerhard Neumann;Georgia Chalvatzaki
abstract: Robot manipulation often fails in the final millimeters: a policy may recognize the right object yet miss the pose offsets, boundaries, or pre-contact alignments needed for action. We argue that such failures arise when semantic invariance suppresses correspondence cues for closed-loop control, or when these cues are not exposed to the policy in a usable form. Modern visual encoders provide strong semantic abstractions, but contact-rich manipulation requires correspondence sensitivity: discriminative feature responses to action-relevant changes in pose, boundary, and contact geometry. Diffusion features provide a strong prior for dense correspondence, but direct use is impractical due to stochasticity, latency, and representation drift. We introduce Robot-DIFT, a deterministic diffusion-derived backbone for real-time control. Through Manifold Distillation, Robot-DIFT converts a noise-conditioned diffusion Teacher into a clean-input, single-pass Student while preserving the teacher's feature manifold. A Spatial-Semantic Feature Pyramid Network (S2-FPN) fuses coarse-to-fine Student decoder features into visual tokens that expose semantic context and fine contact detail to the policy. Across RoboCasa, LIBERO-10, and real robots, Robot-DIFT outperforms vision-language, self-supervised, geometry-oriented, and diffusion baselines on contact-sensitive tasks. Controlled backbone/readout swaps show that S2-FPN unlocks, rather than replaces, the diffusion correspondence prior.
primary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
secondary_keyword: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems

title: DAVATaR: Depth-Aware Visually Augmented Tactile Learning Across the Air-Water Interface
authors: Bowen Jiang;Siqi Shang;Rahul Ajay Iyer;Ashwin Prakash;Lillian Chin;Roberto Martín-Martín
abstract: Manipulation in submerged settings (e.g., washing dishes, bathing, collecting water samples) is difficult because of the air-water interface. Water makes visual cues unreliable and damages electronics. We learn visuo-tactile policies for this regime by fusing visual observations with tactile and immersion-depth signals from a sensorized waterproof gripper. We train imitation learning transformer policies that use submerged-domain visual augmentations to reduce overfitting to turbidity, reflection- and refraction-related artifacts. Across the evaluated submerged manipulation tasks, our full policy achieves a mean success rate of 71%, compared to 41% for the best no-tactile variant. This improvement is especially pronounced under difficult visual conditions, such as floating foam and strong glare. Overall, our results demonstrate combining visual robustness with multimodal tactile sensing improves submerged manipulation. See https://davatar-corl26.github.io/ for details.
primary_keyword: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision
secondary_keyword: Robot systems, hardware, and sensors for learning

title: Learning with Object-centric Representations of Tactile Interactive Perception for Robot Manipulation
authors: Xinyi Yang;Zilin Si;Zhuowei Xu;Zeynep Temel;Oliver Kroemer
abstract: Implicit object properties that are difficult to directly infer from vision, such as material, container contents, or softness, can be revealed through tactile sensing and exploratory interactions. However, because tactile signals are transient and sparse, extracting informative tactile events and effectively incorporating them into robotic manipulation remains a challenge. In this work, we present an object-centric context-aware manipulation framework that learns task-agnostic object representations through tactile exploration. A token learner autonomously selects representative tactile segments from long-horizon exploration, while contrastive alignment with descriptive text embeddings enables a latent space that captures multiple physical object properties. These learned representations are then used as semantic context to guide object-centric manipulation policies and adapt strategies based on object properties. Experiments show that the learned representations achieve 90% accuracy for object property estimation for both seen and unseen objects. Evaluated on three tasks involving visually ambiguous objects, i.e. multi-object rearrangement, pouring, and box opening, the proposed framework improves both target selection and property-dependent manipulation adaptation, achieving an average task success rate of 85%, compared to 36% for baseline policies without object-context conditioning.
primary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
secondary_keyword: Robot manipulation

title: Learning to Assist: Collaborative VLAs for Implicit Human-Robot Collaboration
authors: Leo Xu;Letian Li;Alex Cuellar;Michael Hagenow
abstract: Human-robot collaboration (HRC) combines the complementary strengths of humans and robots to improve task efficiency. However, many existing collaborative systems rely on hand-engineered pipelines, limiting their scalability and flexibility for new tasks. In this work, we show that models trained end-to-end with imitation learning, specifically vision-language-action (VLA) models, can support collaborative manipulation, and characterize the key factors affecting their real-world performance. We evaluate two state-of-the-art models and identify a failure mode of action-chunking policies in implicit HRC, where demonstration action leakage (i.e., action chunks crossing latent task transitions) can cause premature assistive behavior. We find that this issue increases with longer execution horizons and occurs in real-world collaborative VLA systems, such as when a robot attempts to hand over a tool before the person is ready. We propose an inference-time steering method to mitigate these erroneous assistive actions while preserving policy performance. Finally, through a 16-participant user study on a long-horizon collaborative assembly task, we show that steering enables a longer execution horizon while mitigating premature assistance, leading to faster collaboration and fewer failures compared to a shorter-horizon policy.
primary_keyword: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction

title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
authors: Mohammad Omama;Aeyan Ashraf;Sandeep P. Chinchali
abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe "interaction bottleneck." Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a lightweight set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, and ETH3D, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.
primary_keyword: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
secondary_keyword: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

title: Learning Object Manipulation from Scratch via Contrastive Interaction
authors: Tongle Shen;Caleb Chuck;Fan Feng;Biwei Huang
abstract: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CRL) has seen recent success in a wide variety of goal-conditioned robotics tasks by learning structured representations of the dynamics.
